phy_ocra.17.0.summary: In every real system change, some energy is dissipated: it is transferred to the surroundings, usually ending up in their thermal store, so it is stored in less useful ways and is described as wasted. Dissipation is caused by friction, air resistance, electrical resistance, sound and heating of the surroundings. Energy is still conserved; it has simply spread out so it cannot easily do useful work, which is why no real device can be 100% efficient.

core.p: In every real energy transfer, some energy ends up in stores where it is not useful. It spreads out into the surroundings, usually warming them very slightly. This spreading out is called **dissipation**. The energy has not disappeared; it has just been stored in a **less useful way**.
bullets: Energy is **dissipated** when it is transferred to the surroundings and spreads out.
Dissipated energy is usually called **wasted energy**.
It almost always ends up in the **thermal store of the surroundings**.
Once spread out, it is very hard to collect and use again.
Dissipation happens in **all** system changes; no real device avoids it completely.

callouts.p: In all system changes energy is dissipated, so that it is stored in less useful ways; this energy is often described as wasted.

core.p: Dissipation never breaks the law of conservation of energy. The total energy is the same before and after; what changes is how **useful** it is.
bullets: Total energy input = useful energy output + wasted (dissipated) energy.
Wasted energy = total input - useful output.
Energy is never 'lost' or 'used up'; it becomes less concentrated.
A 'closed system' including the surroundings has constant total energy.
The more dissipation, the less of the input does the job you want.

callouts.p: 'The energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings' earns credit; 'the energy is lost' usually does not.

core.p: Whether energy is useful depends on what the device is for. The same transfer can be useful in one device and wasted in another.
bullets: **Useful energy**: transferred to the store we want (e.g. light from a lamp, kinetic from a motor).
**Wasted energy**: transferred to stores we do not want (usually thermal, sometimes sound).
In a heater, the thermal transfer is the useful one.
In a lamp, the thermal transfer is wasted.
In a loudspeaker, sound is useful; in a washing machine, sound is wasted.

core.p: When surfaces rub, work is done against **friction**. This transfers energy to the thermal store of the surfaces, which then heat the surroundings.
bullets: Moving parts in engines, motors and bikes rub together.
Work done against friction raises temperature of the parts.
**Lubrication** (oil, grease) reduces friction between moving parts, so less energy is dissipated.
Brakes deliberately use friction, but the energy still ends up dissipated.

core.h: Causes of dissipation: air resistance and drag
core.p: Moving through air or water means pushing fluid out of the way. Work is done against **air resistance (drag)**, transferring energy to the kinetic and thermal stores of the air.
bullets: Drag increases with speed, so dissipation rises sharply at higher speeds.
**Streamlining** reduces drag, so less energy is wasted.
A pendulum or swing slows down because of air resistance and friction at the pivot.
Cyclists crouch to reduce drag.

fig.cap: A bouncing ball rises less each time. At each impact some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the ball and floor and as sound, and air resistance does work throughout, so less energy is left in the ball's gravitational potential and kinetic stores.

core.p: When a current flows through a wire or component with resistance, the current does work against the resistance, heating the wire. This is why electrical devices warm up.
bullets: Electrons collide with ions in the metal, increasing their vibration (thermal store).
Thick, low-resistance wires dissipate less energy.
Power lines transmit at high voltage and low current to reduce heating losses.
Laptops and phones get warm in use because of resistance in the circuits.

callouts.p: Top answers name the cause (friction, air resistance, electrical resistance) AND the store (thermal store of the surroundings).

core.h: Causes of dissipation: sound and vibration
core.p: Vibrating parts transfer energy to the air as sound waves. Sound spreads out and its energy ends up warming the air.
bullets: Loud engines and machines dissipate energy as sound.
Eventually sound energy is absorbed and becomes thermal energy of the surroundings.
Securing loose parts and using rubber mounts reduce vibration and noise.

core.h: Causes of dissipation: heating the surroundings
core.p: Any object hotter than its surroundings transfers energy to them by heating (conduction, convection, radiation). In a house, kettle or engine this is wasted energy.
bullets: A hot drink cools as energy is dissipated to the room.
Hot engines lose energy through their casing and exhaust gases.
Thermal insulation slows this transfer (covered fully in P7.2f-g).
The bigger the temperature difference, the faster the energy is dissipated.

core.h: Why dissipated energy is less useful
core.p: Useful energy is concentrated: in a fuel, a battery, a hot object or a moving car. After dissipation the same energy is shared among a huge number of particles, each gaining a tiny amount. A tiny temperature rise in a big room cannot boil a kettle or drive a motor.
bullets: Concentrated energy can be transferred to do useful work.
Spread-out energy at a temperature close to the surroundings cannot easily do work.
This is why we keep needing fresh fuel even though energy is conserved.
Energy naturally tends to spread out; it never 'un-spreads' on its own.

callouts.p: Dissipated does not mean destroyed. It means spread out and less useful.

core.p: A **Sankey diagram** shows the input, useful and wasted energy. The width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy, so you can see at a glance how much is dissipated.
bullets: Input arrow on the left; useful output straight on; wasted output bends off (usually downward).
Widths of outputs add up to the width of the input (conservation of energy).
Use the scale (e.g. 1 square = 10 J) to read values.
A wide wasted arrow means lots of dissipation and a low efficiency.

fig.cap: Sankey diagram for a filament lamp. Arrow width is proportional to energy. Of every 100 J transferred electrically, only 10 J is useful light; 90 J heats the lamp and is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings. Total out = total in (conservation).

core.p: Because of dissipation, no real device transfers all its input energy usefully. Efficiency measures what fraction is useful (fully covered in P7.2d-e).
bullets: Efficiency = useful output energy transfer / input energy transfer.
More dissipation means lower efficiency.
No device can be 100% efficient, because some dissipation always occurs.
Exception in effect: an electric heater is close to 100% efficient because the 'waste' (heating) is the useful output.

core.p: Explain dissipation with a chain: cause -> work done -> store -> spreading -> less useful -> conservation.
bullets: Example: 'Work is done against friction in the bearings, transferring energy to the thermal store of the motor; this is dissipated to the surroundings so it is less useful, but the total energy is conserved.'
Always give an example when the question says 'with examples'.
Name the useful store as well as the wasted one.
Never write 'energy is lost as heat'; write 'dissipated by heating to the thermal store of the surroundings'.

analogy.t: Spilling a bag of sweets on a beach
analogy.p: Useful energy is like a full bag of sweets in your hand: concentrated and ready to share out exactly where you want. Each time energy is transferred, a few sweets fall through a hole and scatter across the sand. None of the sweets vanish (conservation), but scattered sweets are almost impossible to gather back up (less useful). Friction, resistance and air resistance are the holes in the bag. The analogy breaks down because sweets are separate objects that could in principle be collected, whereas dissipated energy is shared as tiny extra motion of countless particles and cannot be gathered back without using even more energy.

Everything outside the device or system, such as the air and nearby objects.
A force opposing motion between surfaces in contact; work against it dissipates energy as thermal energy.
A frictional force on objects moving through air; it increases with speed.
Opposition to current; causes heating when current flows.
Using oil or grease between moving surfaces to reduce friction and so reduce dissipation.
Shaping an object to reduce air resistance.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred, stored or dissipated.
A diagram whose arrow widths are proportional to energy, showing input, useful and wasted energy.

mistakes.w: Energy is lost as heat.
mistakes.r: Energy is dissipated by heating to the thermal store of the surroundings.

mistakes.w: Wasted energy is destroyed.
mistakes.r: It still exists but is spread out and less useful.

mistakes.w: Dissipation breaks conservation of energy.
mistakes.r: Total energy is unchanged; useful + wasted = input.

mistakes.w: Heat energy is a store.
mistakes.r: The store is the thermal store; heating is the transfer process.

mistakes.w: A good machine has no wasted energy.
mistakes.r: All real machines dissipate some energy; none is 100% efficient.

mistakes.w: Sound is a useful output for all devices.
mistakes.r: Sound is useful only if the device is meant to make it (e.g. a speaker).

mistakes.w: Lubrication removes friction.
mistakes.r: Lubrication reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated.

mistakes.w: The wasted arrow in a Sankey can be any width.
mistakes.r: The output arrows must add up to the input width.

exam.q: What is meant by energy being dissipated?
model: Energy is spread out / transferred to the surroundings so it is stored in a less useful way.
exam.tip: Mention 'less useful' or 'spread out'.

exam.q: Name the store that most wasted energy ends up in.
model: Thermal store (of the surroundings).
exam.tip: Not 'heat'.

exam.q: Give two causes of energy dissipation in a bicycle.
model: Friction between moving parts (chain, axle, brakes).
Air resistance.
exam.tip: Different causes for each mark.

exam.q: A lamp is supplied with 60 J. 12 J is transferred as light. Calculate the energy dissipated and state where it goes.
model: To the thermal store of the lamp and surroundings.
exam.tip: Use conservation.

exam.q: Explain why a swinging pendulum eventually stops.
model: Work is done against air resistance / friction at the pivot.
Energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings (dissipated).
So the pendulum's kinetic and gravitational stores decrease until it stops.
exam.tip: Total energy is still conserved.

exam.q: Explain why energy that has been dissipated is less useful.
model: It is spread out among many particles / over a large area.
Each gains only a small amount (small temperature rise), so it cannot be used to do useful work.
exam.tip: Idea of concentration.

exam.q: Explain how lubrication reduces energy dissipation in a machine.
model: Lubricant reduces friction between moving parts.
Less work is done against friction so less energy is transferred to the thermal store.
exam.tip: Link method to reduced work against friction.

exam.q: Describe where energy is dissipated in an electric motor.
model: Current in coils heats wires due to resistance.
Friction in the bearings/axle heats moving parts.
Vibration produces sound.
All ends in the thermal store of the surroundings.
exam.tip: One cause per mark plus where it ends.

exam.q: A student says energy is 'used up' when a car travels along a road. Evaluate this statement using ideas about dissipation and conservation of energy.
model: Energy is not used up; it cannot be created or destroyed.
Chemical store of the fuel decreases.
Energy is transferred by work against friction and air resistance and by heating in the engine.
It ends up dissipated in the thermal store of the surroundings, less useful but still present.
exam.tip: Evaluate: say why the student is wrong and correct them.

exam.q: Explain, with examples, why in all system changes some energy is dissipated, and why this means no device can be 100% efficient.
model: Whenever energy is transferred, forces such as friction or air resistance do work, or currents heat resistances.
Example: friction in a car engine heats moving parts.
Example: a filament lamp heats up as current flows through it.
This energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings and spreads out.
Dissipated energy is stored in less useful ways / wasted.
Because some energy is always dissipated, useful output is always less than input, so efficiency is less than 100%.
exam.tip: Give at least two different examples.

worked.q: An electric motor is supplied with 500 J. It does 350 J of useful work lifting a load. Calculate the energy dissipated and describe where it goes.
steps: Some heats the coils through electrical resistance.
Some heats the bearings through friction; a little is transferred as sound.
All 150 J eventually ends up in the thermal store of the surroundings.
worked.ans: 150 J dissipated, mostly to the thermal store of the surroundings.

worked.q: A ball dropped from 2.0 m bounces back to 1.5 m. What fraction of its energy was dissipated, and why?
steps: GPE is proportional to height (GPE = mgh).
Dissipated by deformation at impact heating the ball and floor, sound, and air resistance.
worked.ans: 0.25 (25%) of the energy is dissipated, mainly to thermal stores of the ball, floor and air.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a hot cup of tea left on a table eventually reaches room temperature but the room does not noticeably warm.
steps: Energy is transferred by heating from the hot tea to the cooler surroundings.
The energy spreads out among a huge number of air particles and the table.
Each particle gains only a tiny amount of energy, so the room's temperature rise is too small to notice.
The energy is conserved but dissipated: stored in a less useful way.
worked.ans: Energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings; spread so thinly that the temperature rise is negligible.

phy_ocra.17.1.summary: Domestic appliances take energy from the mains electrically and transfer it to useful stores such as the thermal store of water or the kinetic store of a motor, with some always dissipated. Power is the rate of energy transfer: power = energy transferred / time, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). An appliance's power rating tells you how quickly its stores change: a higher power rating means more energy transferred each second, so the same energy change happens in less time.

core.p: Every domestic appliance takes energy from the mains (or a battery) **electrically**, because the current does work in the appliance. That energy is then transferred to other stores, some usefully and some dissipated.
bullets: Kettle: electrically -> thermal store of the heating element -> by heating to the **thermal store of the water**.
Electric fan / drill / washing machine motor: electrically -> **kinetic store** of moving parts.
Lamp: electrically -> light radiated (useful) and thermal store of surroundings (wasted).
Television: electrically -> light and sound (useful), thermal (wasted).
Charging a phone: electrically -> **chemical store** of the battery.
In every case some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings.

Main useful store / transfer
Wasted

Thermal store of air and kinetic store of air
Kinetic store of motor and air
Thermal store of bread; infrared radiated

core.p: Power tells you **how quickly** energy is transferred, not how much. Two appliances might transfer the same total energy, but the higher-power one does it faster.
bullets: **Power is the rate of energy transfer** (or the rate of doing work).
Unit: **watt (W)**. **1 W = 1 joule per second (1 J/s)**.
1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W; 1 megawatt (MW) = 1 000 000 W.
A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J every second.
Higher power = more energy transferred each second.

callouts.p: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or the rate at which work is done; power = energy transferred / time.

core.p: You must recall and use the equation linking power, energy and time, and its rearranged forms.
bullets: **Power (W) = energy transferred (J) / time (s)**, P = E / t.
Also **power (W) = work done (J) / time (s)**.
Rearranged: **E = P x t** and **t = E / P**.
Time must be in **seconds**: 1 minute = 60 s, 1 hour = 3600 s.
Power in **watts**: convert kW to W (x 1000).

callouts.p: Using minutes instead of seconds is the most common error. 5 minutes = 300 s.

core.p: Every appliance has a **power rating** printed on it, telling you the energy it transfers per second when working normally. The power rating links directly to how quickly its energy stores change.
bullets: The higher the power rating, the faster energy is transferred from the mains to the appliance's stores.
Heating appliances (kettles, ovens, heaters, hairdryers, showers) have high ratings (1 to 10 kW).
Lighting and electronics have low ratings (a few W to a few hundred W).
Energy transferred depends on BOTH power and time the appliance is used: E = P x t.
A low-power appliance left on for a long time can transfer more energy than a high-power one used briefly.

callouts.p: The power rating is NOT the energy used. Energy depends on how long it runs.

core.h: Relating power to changes in stored energy
core.p: OCR asks you to describe the link between power rating and changes in stored energy when an appliance is in use. A higher-power appliance increases the useful store faster.
bullets: A 3 kW kettle raises the thermal store of water twice as fast as a 1.5 kW kettle, so it boils the same water in about half the time.
A more powerful motor increases the kinetic store (or lifts a load, increasing GPE) more quickly.
For the same task (same energy change), time = energy / power, so doubling power halves the time.
In the same time, doubling the power doubles the energy transferred.
Some of the transferred energy is always dissipated, so the useful store gains less than P x t.

callouts.p: Use proportional reasoning: 'twice the power means twice the energy per second, so half the time for the same energy change'.

core.p: Electrical power can also be calculated from current and potential difference. These link this point to circuits.
bullets: **Power (W) = potential difference (V) x current (A)**, P = I x V.
**Power (W) = current^2 (A^2) x resistance (ohms)**, P = I^2 x R.
**Energy transferred (J) = charge (C) x potential difference (V)**, E = Q x V.
Combining: E = I x V x t.
UK mains supply is about 230 V a.c., so a kettle drawing 13 A has power of about 3000 W.

core.p: Electricity companies measure energy in **kilowatt-hours (kWh)** because joules are too small for household amounts.
bullets: Energy (kWh) = power (kW) x time (h).
1 kWh is the energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour.
Cost = number of kWh x price per kWh.
Reducing power or time of use reduces energy transferred and cost.

callouts.p: Use kW and hours together for kWh, or W and seconds together for J. Never mix them.

core.h: Practical (PAG P5): measuring the power of an appliance
core.p: You can find the power of a heater or low-voltage appliance by measuring the energy it transfers in a measured time.
bullets: Connect the appliance through a **joulemeter** (or an ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel).
Switch on and start a stopwatch; record energy after a measured time.
Power = energy / time; or P = I x V from the meter readings.
Repeat and take a mean to reduce random errors.
Compare with the stated power rating; differences come from meter uncertainty and supply voltage variations.
Safety: heaters get hot, so do not touch, and use low-voltage supplies.

core.p: Running up stairs does work against gravity, increasing your GPE store. Measuring how quickly you do this gives your power output.
bullets: Measure your mass (kg) on bathroom scales; weight = m x g.
Measure vertical height of the stairs (height of one step x number of steps).
Time how long it takes to climb with a stopwatch.
Work done = GPE gained = m x g x h; power = work done / time.
Repeat and average; walking vs running shows the same work but different power.
This underestimates true power because energy is also dissipated in muscles and as kinetic energy.

core.p: Power ratings help consumers compare appliances and their energy use.
bullets: Lower power appliances that do the same job (e.g. LED vs filament lamp) transfer less energy, costing less.
A higher power kettle boils water faster but transfers about the same total energy for the same water.
Appliances on standby still transfer small amounts of energy continuously.
Energy ratings (A to G) indicate how efficiently appliances transfer energy usefully.

core.p: Power questions are often multi-step and combine power with other equations.
bullets: Write the equation, substitute with units, calculate, then give the unit.
Check time is in seconds and power in watts before using E = P x t.
For two-step questions, find energy first (e.g. GPE = mgh) then divide by time.
Give answers in standard form or kJ/MJ if numbers are large: 1 800 000 J = 1.8 MJ.
Sense-check: a kettle should transfer hundreds of thousands of joules in a few minutes.

analogy.p: Think of energy as water and the appliance's useful store as a bath. The power rating is how far the tap is turned on: a 3 kW kettle is a tap on full, an LED lamp is a slow drip. The total water in the bath depends on both the flow rate and how long the tap runs (E = P x t), so a dripping tap left on all week can fill more than a gushing tap opened for a minute. A small leak in the bath stands for dissipated energy. The analogy breaks down because water is a substance that flows through pipes, whereas energy is not a fluid; the current in the wires carries charge, not 'energy particles'.

terms.d: The rate of energy transfer or rate of doing work; P = E / t.
Unit of power; 1 W = 1 J transferred per second.
1000 watts.
The power of an appliance when operating normally, stated by the manufacturer.
Amount of energy moved between stores, in joules; E = P x t.
Energy transferred by a force moving an object; equal to energy transferred.
Energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour; 3.6 MJ.
A meter that measures the electrical energy transferred to an appliance.
Rate of flow of charge, in amperes (A).
Energy transferred per unit charge between two points, in volts (V).
UK supply of about 230 V a.c. at 50 Hz.
Energy of particles of a substance; increases with temperature.
Energy spread to the surroundings and stored in less useful ways.
How much of something happens per unit of time.

mistakes.w: Power is the amount of energy an appliance uses.
mistakes.r: Power is the rate of energy transfer: energy per second.

mistakes.w: Using time in minutes in P = E / t.
mistakes.r: Convert time to seconds.

mistakes.w: A higher power kettle uses more energy to boil the same water.
mistakes.r: It transfers energy faster, so boils the water in less time; total useful energy is about the same.

mistakes.w: Mixing kW with seconds to get joules.
mistakes.r: Use W with seconds for J, or kW with hours for kWh.

mistakes.w: Electrical energy is stored in the appliance.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred electrically to stores such as the thermal store of water.

mistakes.w: Using the distance along the stairs in personal power.
mistakes.r: Use vertical height: work done = mgh.

mistakes.w: Power unit is J.
mistakes.r: Power is measured in watts (W), J/s.

exam.q: State the unit of power.
model: Watt (W) / J/s.
exam.tip: Either accepted.

exam.q: Write down the equation linking power, energy transferred and time.
model: Power = energy transferred / time.
exam.tip: Must be recalled.

exam.q: Describe the useful energy transfer in an electric kettle.
model: Energy is transferred electrically to the heating element.
Then by heating to the thermal store of the water.
exam.tip: Name the pathway and the store.

exam.q: A 2000 W hairdryer is used for 5 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.
exam.tip: Convert minutes first.

exam.q: A lamp transfers 9000 J in 15 minutes. Calculate its power.
exam.tip: Give the unit.

exam.q: Kettle A is rated 3 kW, kettle B 1.5 kW. Explain which boils 1 litre of water faster.
model: Kettle A has higher power so transfers energy at a faster rate / more energy per second.
Same energy needed, so A takes about half the time.
exam.tip: Use 'rate'.

exam.q: A 3 kW heater is on for 4 hours. Electricity costs 30p per kWh. Calculate the cost.
model: Energy = 3 x 4 = 12 kWh
Cost = 12 x 30
= 360p (3.60 pounds)
exam.tip: Keep kW and hours together.

exam.q: A 60 kg student runs up stairs of vertical height 4 m in 6 s. g = 10 N/kg. Calculate their power.
model: Work done = mgh = 60 x 10 x 4 = 2400 J
exam.tip: Two-step: energy first.

exam.q: A motor lifts a 50 N load through 3 m in 10 s. Calculate the useful power output and suggest why the electrical power input is greater.
model: Work done = F x d = 50 x 3 = 150 J
Input power greater because energy is dissipated
by friction / resistance heating the motor and surroundings (and sound).
exam.tip: Link to dissipation.

exam.q: Describe how you would measure the power of a small electric heater in the laboratory. Include the measurements, equipment and how to calculate power.
model: Connect the heater to a low-voltage supply through a joulemeter (or ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel).
Switch on and start a stopwatch at the same time.
Record the energy transferred (joulemeter reading) after a measured time, e.g. 5 minutes.
Convert time to seconds.
Power = energy / time (or P = I x V).
Repeat and calculate a mean; take care, the heater gets hot.
exam.tip: Name equipment, measurements and equation.

A microwave transfers 540 000 J while heating a meal for 9 minutes. What is its power rating? How long would a 900 W microwave take for the same energy?
steps: 600 s = 10 minutes: lower power, longer time for the same energy change.

phy_ocra.17.2.summary: **Efficiency** tells you what fraction of the energy put into a device ends up being transferred usefully. OCR expects you to recall and use efficiency = useful output energy transfer / input energy transfer, express it as a decimal or percentage, and explain practical ways of increasing efficiency by reducing the energy that is dissipated (wasted) to the surroundings, usually as thermal energy through friction, air resistance, electrical resistance or poor insulation.

core.p: Every real device takes in energy and transfers some of it to the store we want (useful) and the rest to stores we do not want, usually the **thermal store of the surroundings**. Efficiency compares the useful output with the total input.
bullets: Energy is **conserved**: input energy = useful output + wasted output.
Wasted energy is **dissipated**: spread out to the surroundings, so it is much less useful.
Efficiency has **no units**: it is a ratio of two energies (or two powers).
It can be written as a decimal (0.35) or a percentage (35%).
A higher efficiency means a **greater proportion** of the input is transferred usefully.

callouts.p: efficiency = useful output energy transfer (J) / input energy transfer (J)

core.p: This is an equation OCR expects you to **recall and apply**. Both energies must be in the same unit so the units cancel.
bullets: efficiency = useful output energy transfer / input energy transfer
percentage efficiency = (useful output / input) x 100
Rearranged: useful output = efficiency x input
Rearranged: input = useful output / efficiency
Use the decimal form (not the percentage) when rearranging, e.g. 40% = 0.40.

callouts.p: Efficiency can never be more than 1 (100%). If you get more than 1, you have divided the wrong way round.

core.p: Power is energy transferred per second, so the same ratio works with powers: useful power output / total power input. The seconds cancel out, giving the same efficiency.
bullets: efficiency = useful power output (W) / total power input (W)
Useful because appliances are labelled with **power ratings**, not energies.
Power and energy versions agree because energy = power x time and the time is the same for both.
Watch units: change kW to W (x 1000) before dividing only if the two are in different units.

callouts.p: Using powers or energies gives the same efficiency, as long as both are measured over the same time.

core.p: In any real energy transfer some energy is always dissipated, mainly by heating the device and its surroundings. This is why efficiency is always less than 100% (except for electric heaters where heating is the useful output).
bullets: **Friction** between moving parts heats them up.
**Air resistance (drag)** does work against motion, heating the air.
**Electrical resistance** in wires and coils causes heating when a current flows.
**Sound** produced by vibrations is usually wasted and ends as thermal energy.
Hot parts lose energy to cooler surroundings by **conduction, convection and radiation**.

callouts.p: Wasted energy is not lost from the universe; it is dissipated into the thermal store of the surroundings.

core.p: A Sankey diagram shows energy transfers as arrows whose **width is proportional to the amount of energy**. The input arrow splits into useful and wasted arrows, and the widths of the outputs add up to the input.
bullets: Useful output usually continues straight on; wasted output bends away (often downwards).
Read the energy from the width using the scale given.
Efficiency = width of useful arrow / width of input arrow.
A wide wasted arrow means low efficiency.

callouts.p: Always check: input = sum of outputs. Examiners often ask for a missing value.

core.p: Efficiency lets you compare devices fairly, even when they have different inputs. The device with the larger fraction of useful output is more efficient, and it costs less to run for the same useful job.
bullets: An **LED** transfers a much larger proportion of its input to light than a **filament lamp**, so it is more efficient.
A more efficient appliance needs **less input energy** for the same useful output.
Less input energy means **lower running costs** and, if electricity comes from fossil fuels, fewer emissions.
Compare efficiencies as decimals or percentages, never just by the size of the wasted energy alone.

core.p: Friction between moving surfaces does work that heats them. **Lubricating** moving parts with oil or grease reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated as thermal energy and a greater proportion is transferred usefully.
bullets: Oil forms a thin layer that keeps surfaces apart.
Used in engines, bike chains, gears, motors and hinges.
Reducing friction also reduces wear and noise.
Ball bearings and smooth surfaces also reduce friction.

callouts.p: Lubrication -> less friction -> less energy dissipated as heat -> more useful output for same input -> higher efficiency.

core.p: When the useful output is keeping something hot (or cold), energy leaks out through the walls. **Thermal insulation** reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating, so less input energy is wasted.
bullets: Insulated kettles, ovens and hot water tanks keep more energy in the useful thermal store.
Insulators are materials with **low thermal conductivity**, often trapping air.
Lids reduce energy lost by evaporation and convection.
Shiny surfaces reduce energy lost by infrared radiation.

core.h: Increasing efficiency: streamlining and lower resistance
core.p: For moving vehicles, **streamlining** reduces air resistance so less energy is transferred to the air. For electrical devices, using wires with **low resistance** reduces heating in the wires.
bullets: Streamlined shapes let air flow smoothly around a car, train or cyclist.
Thicker wires or better conductors (e.g. copper) have lower resistance.
Less current, or lower resistance, means less heating in cables.
Replacing a device with a better design (e.g. filament to LED) is also a way to increase efficiency.

core.p: Being able to describe the energy transfers in a device is the first step to explaining its efficiency.
bullets: Electric motor lifting a load: energy transferred electrically -> gravitational potential energy store of the load (useful).
Wasted: thermal store of motor and surroundings (friction, resistance), and sound.
To improve: lubricate the bearings, use low-resistance coils, reduce vibration.

callouts.p: Use store words: kinetic, gravitational potential, thermal, chemical. Use transfer words: electrically, mechanically, by heating, by radiation.

core.p: Whether an output is useful depends on the purpose of the device. In an electric heater the thermal output is the useful output, so its efficiency is close to 100%.
bullets: Heater: useful output = thermal store of the room.
Some light from a glowing heater element is not useful but still ends up warming the room.
In a lamp, heating is wasted; in a heater, it is useful.

callouts.p: Always decide what the device is for before labelling outputs as useful or wasted.

core.p: Efficiency questions mix calculation with explanation. Lay out your working clearly and finish explanations with the effect on efficiency.
bullets: Write the equation, substitute with units, then give the answer.
State whether your answer is a decimal or a percentage.
If asked 'how could efficiency be increased', name the method AND say which wasted transfer it reduces.
Round sensibly, usually 2 or 3 significant figures.

analogy.p: Think of input energy as water poured into a leaky watering can to water a plant. The water reaching the plant is the useful output; the water dripping out of holes onto the path is wasted energy. Efficiency is the fraction that reaches the plant. Patching holes (lubrication, insulation, streamlining) means more of the same water reaches the plant. Where it breaks down: spilt water can be collected and reused, but dissipated energy is spread so thinly into the surroundings that it is practically impossible to use again.

terms.d: The ratio of useful output energy transfer to input energy transfer; has no units.
The energy transferred to the store that the device is designed to fill.
The total energy supplied to a device.
Energy transferred to stores that are not wanted, usually the thermal store of the surroundings.
The spreading out of energy into the surroundings so it becomes less useful.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores.
A diagram where arrow widths are proportional to the amounts of energy transferred.
The rate of energy transfer, measured in watts (W); 1 W = 1 J/s.
A force opposing relative motion between surfaces that causes heating.
Adding oil or grease between moving parts to reduce friction.
A material or method that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating.
Shaping an object so air or water flows smoothly around it, reducing drag.
Opposition to current that causes heating when charge flows through a component.
Efficiency multiplied by 100 and expressed with a % sign.

mistakes.w: Efficiency = input / useful output
mistakes.r: efficiency = useful output / input; it must be 1 or less.

mistakes.w: The wasted energy is lost / destroyed.
mistakes.r: The wasted energy is dissipated to the surroundings (thermal store); energy is conserved.

mistakes.w: Efficiency = 0.25 J
mistakes.r: Efficiency has no units: 0.25 or 25%.

mistakes.w: Using 40 instead of 0.40 when rearranging, getting huge answers.
mistakes.r: Convert percentage to decimal first: 40% = 0.40.

mistakes.w: Lubrication increases efficiency because it adds energy.
mistakes.r: Lubrication reduces friction so less energy is dissipated as heat; a greater proportion of input is useful.

mistakes.w: A device that wastes 50 J is less efficient than one that wastes 20 J.
mistakes.r: You must compare proportions: efficiency depends on wasted energy relative to the input.

mistakes.w: Insulation stops heat escaping.
mistakes.r: Insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating; it does not stop it completely.

mistakes.w: A machine can be 100% efficient if it is well designed.
mistakes.r: Some energy is always dissipated (e.g. by friction or heating), so efficiency is always less than 100% for a mechanical device.

exam.q: State the equation that links efficiency, useful output energy transfer and input energy transfer.
model: efficiency = useful output energy transfer / input energy transfer
exam.tip: Word equations score; symbols must be correct if used.

exam.q: A motor is supplied with 500 J and transfers 350 J to the kinetic store. Calculate its efficiency.
model: efficiency = 350 / 500
exam.tip: Show the substitution for the first mark.

exam.q: A kettle is 80% efficient. It transfers 240 000 J to the water. Calculate the energy supplied to the kettle.
model: input = useful output / efficiency
exam.tip: Use the decimal 0.80, not 80.

exam.q: A filament lamp has an input of 60 J each second and gives out 3 J of light each second. Calculate the energy wasted each second and the efficiency.
model: wasted = 60 - 3 = 57 J
efficiency = 3 / 60
exam.tip: Conservation of energy gives the wasted energy.

exam.q: Explain why an electric motor is less than 100% efficient.
model: friction in bearings / resistance in coils causes heating
so some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings (or as sound)
exam.tip: Name the cause and where the energy goes.

exam.q: Suggest one way of increasing the efficiency of a bicycle and explain how it works.
model: lubricate the chain / gears
reduces friction so less energy dissipated as heat
exam.tip: Method plus effect on wasted energy.

exam.q: A heater is 100% efficient but a lamp is not. Explain why.
model: the useful output of a heater is thermal energy
any energy dissipated as heat is still useful, whereas in a lamp heating is wasted
exam.tip: Useful depends on purpose.

exam.q: An LED lamp and a filament lamp give out the same amount of light. Explain why the LED is cheaper to run.
model: LED is more efficient
so wastes less energy as heat
so needs a smaller input energy / power for the same light, so costs less
exam.tip: Link efficiency to input energy and cost.

exam.q: A crane motor has a useful power output of 4.5 kW and a total power input of 6.0 kW. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage. (Higher)
model: efficiency = 4.5 / 6.0 = 0.75
exam.tip: Units match (both kW) so no conversion needed.

exam.q: Describe and explain ways in which the efficiency of a car can be increased.
model: lubricate moving engine parts
reduces friction so less energy dissipated by heating
streamline the body shape
reduces air resistance so less energy transferred to the air
insulate / reduce heat loss from the engine or use a more efficient engine design
so a greater proportion of the chemical energy input is transferred to the kinetic store
exam.tip: For 6 marks give at least three methods, each with a clear explanation linked to efficiency.

worked.q: An electric motor is supplied with 2400 J of energy. It lifts a load, increasing its gravitational potential energy store by 1800 J. Calculate the efficiency and the energy wasted.
steps: Write the equation: efficiency = useful output / input
worked.ans: Efficiency = 0.75 (75%); 600 J wasted, mostly as thermal energy and sound.

worked.q: A power station is 35% efficient and supplies 700 MJ of electrical energy. How much energy was stored in the fuel used?
worked.ans: 2000 MJ (2.0 x 10^9 J) of chemical energy was used.

worked.q: After lubrication, the motor above wastes only 300 J for the same 2400 J input. Calculate the new efficiency and explain the change.
steps: Lubrication reduced friction, so less energy was dissipated by heating
worked.ans: Efficiency rises from 75% to 87.5% because less energy is wasted by friction.

phy_ocra.17.3.summary: Unwanted energy transfers waste energy, usually by heating the surroundings. OCR expects you to explain how they can be reduced, for example by **lubrication** (less friction) and **thermal insulation** (slower energy transfer by heating). For buildings you must describe, qualitatively, how the **rate of cooling** depends on the **thickness** and **thermal conductivity** of the walls, and be able to plan and analyse a PAG P5 investigation comparing thermal insulators.

core.p: In any system some energy is transferred to stores we do not want, usually the **thermal store of the surroundings**. This energy is **dissipated** (spread out) and cannot easily be used again, so we try to reduce these unwanted transfers.
bullets: Friction between moving parts transfers energy by heating.
Hot objects (houses, kettles, pipes) transfer energy to cooler surroundings.
Energy is still conserved: it is not destroyed, just wasted.
Reducing unwanted transfers increases efficiency and saves money.
The two methods named by OCR are **lubrication** and **thermal insulation**.

core.p: When surfaces rub together, friction does work that heats them. A **lubricant** such as oil or grease forms a thin layer between the surfaces, so they slide more easily.
bullets: Reduces **friction** between moving parts.
So less energy is dissipated by heating (and less as sound).
Examples: engine oil, grease on bike chains, oiled hinges and gears.
Also reduces wear on parts, so machines last longer.

callouts.p: Lubricate -> less friction -> less energy transferred to thermal store -> less unwanted energy transfer.

core.p: Thermal insulation reduces the **rate** at which energy is transferred by heating from a hotter place to a colder place. It never stops the transfer completely, but slows it down.
bullets: Insulators have a **low thermal conductivity**.
Many insulators work by trapping **air**, which is a poor conductor.
Trapping the air in small pockets also stops **convection** currents forming.
Shiny or light surfaces reduce energy transfer by **infrared radiation**.
Examples: lagging on hot water tanks, wool clothing, vacuum flasks, loft insulation.

callouts.p: A material with a low thermal conductivity that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating.

core.p: **Thermal conductivity** is a property of a material that describes how well it conducts energy by heating. A material with a **higher thermal conductivity** transfers energy through it at a **higher rate** (for the same thickness and temperature difference).
bullets: Metals (copper, aluminium) have high thermal conductivity.
Brick, glass and wood have lower thermal conductivity.
Air, foam, fibreglass and wool have very low thermal conductivity.
Thermal conductivity is a property of the material, not of the object's size.

callouts.p: A measure of how well a material transfers energy by conduction; the higher it is, the higher the rate of energy transfer through the material.

core.h: Rate of cooling of a building: wall thickness
core.p: A house is warmer than the air outside, so energy is transferred out through the walls, roof, windows and floor. The **thicker** the walls, the **lower the rate** of energy transfer through them, so the building **cools more slowly**.
bullets: Energy has further to travel through a thick wall.
Thicker walls -> lower rate of energy transfer -> slower rate of cooling.
This is a **qualitative** relationship: you describe it, you are not expected to calculate it.
Slower cooling means the heating system needs to supply less energy to keep the house warm.

core.h: Rate of cooling of a building: thermal conductivity
core.p: Walls made from materials with a **lower thermal conductivity** transfer energy more slowly, so the building cools more slowly. Combining thick walls with low conductivity materials gives the slowest cooling.
bullets: Lower thermal conductivity -> lower rate of energy transfer -> slower cooling.
Higher thermal conductivity -> higher rate of energy transfer -> faster cooling.
The bigger the temperature difference between inside and outside, the faster the energy transfer.
A larger surface area of wall or window also increases the rate of energy transfer.

callouts.p: In longer answers say both: thicker walls AND lower thermal conductivity reduce the rate of cooling.

core.p: Home insulation methods all reduce the rate of energy transfer out of the house, so less energy (and money) is needed for heating.
bullets: Each method either uses a low thermal conductivity material, traps air, or blocks air flow.
Warm air rises, so a lot of energy is lost through the roof: loft insulation is very effective.
Draughts carry warm air out by convection; draught excluders block gaps.

head: Method
How it reduces energy transfer
rows: Traps air in fibres; low conductivity; reduces conduction and convection through roof
Fills gap between walls with foam that traps air; stops convection in the cavity
Gap of air or gas between panes has low conductivity; reduces conduction
Block gaps so warm air cannot escape by convection
Trap air layers; reduce conduction and convection
Lower rate of conduction through the wall

core.h: Why trapped air is such a good insulator
core.p: Gases have particles that are far apart, so they are poor conductors. But air can move and form convection currents. Insulators like foam, wool and fibreglass trap air in tiny pockets so it **cannot move**, which reduces both conduction and convection.
bullets: Particles in a gas collide less often, so conduction is slow.
Trapped air cannot circulate, so convection is prevented.
This is why a cavity full of foam insulates better than an empty cavity.
Fluffy materials insulate well because they contain lots of trapped air.

callouts.t: Air is not a 'bad conductor of cold'
callouts.p: Never talk about cold flowing in. Energy is transferred from hot to cold, so insulation keeps energy in.

core.p: In this practical you compare how well different materials insulate by measuring how quickly hot water cools in a beaker wrapped with each material.
bullets: Wrap a beaker in one layer of the test material (e.g. bubble wrap, cotton wool, newspaper, foam).
Pour in a measured **volume** of hot water (e.g. 200 cm3) from a kettle.
Put a lid on and insert a thermometer; record the starting temperature.
Record the temperature every minute (or after a fixed time, e.g. 10 minutes) using a stopwatch.
Repeat with the other materials and with no insulation as a control.
Alternatively, test different **thicknesses** (number of layers) of the same material.

callouts.p: Hot water can scald: stand up, keep the beaker on a heatproof mat, and pour carefully.

core.p: To make it a fair test, only the insulating material (or its thickness) is changed.
bullets: Independent variable: type of insulating material (or number of layers).
Dependent variable: temperature drop in a fixed time (or rate of cooling).
Control variables: volume of water, starting temperature, size and type of beaker, thickness of material, lid on, room temperature, time interval.
A control (no insulation) gives a comparison.

callouts.p: Start each test at the same temperature, because hotter water cools faster due to the larger temperature difference.

core.p: Plot **temperature (y-axis) against time (x-axis)** for each material. The best insulator gives the **smallest temperature drop** in the same time, which is the **least steep** cooling curve.
bullets: Cooling curves get less steep over time because the temperature difference with the room gets smaller.
Compare the temperature drop over the same time interval.
The material with the lowest thermal conductivity (or thickest layer) gives the slowest cooling.
More layers give a smaller temperature drop, showing the effect of thickness.

fig.cap: Cooling curves: water in an uninsulated beaker cools quickly (steep red curve), while insulated water cools slowly (shallow green curve). Both curves level off towards room temperature.

core.p: Good evaluation spots sources of error and suggests specific improvements.
bullets: Energy lost while transferring water and before the lid goes on: work quickly and consistently.
Reading error on a thermometer: use a digital temperature probe and data logger.
Different thicknesses of material: measure and keep the thickness the same.
Repeat each test and calculate a mean to improve reliability (repeatability).

core.h: Reducing unwanted transfers saves money and energy
core.p: Insulation and lubrication both mean less input energy is needed for the same useful job, so fuel bills and environmental impact are reduced.
bullets: A house that cools more slowly needs less fuel to keep it warm.
Less fuel burned means fewer carbon dioxide emissions.
Cost-effectiveness: compare installation cost with yearly savings (payback time = cost / yearly saving).

analogy.p: Imagine the energy in a warm house as a crowd of people trying to leave a stadium through the walls. A thin wall is like a short corridor: people get out fast. A thick wall is a long corridor: it takes longer, so fewer leave each minute. Thermal conductivity is how clear the corridor is: high conductivity is an empty, wide corridor, low conductivity is one crammed with obstacles (like trapped air pockets). Where it breaks down: energy is not made of particles that walk out; energy is passed on by vibrating particles colliding, and the flow depends on the temperature difference, not on people choosing to leave.

terms.d: Energy transferred to a store that is not useful, usually the thermal store of the surroundings.
Spreading of energy into the surroundings so it becomes less useful.
Adding oil or grease between surfaces to reduce friction.
A force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact and causes heating.
Material or method that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating.
How well a material conducts energy by heating; higher conductivity means a higher rate of energy transfer.
Energy transfer by heating through a material by particles vibrating and colliding (and free electrons in metals).
Energy transfer in a fluid where warmer, less dense fluid rises and cooler fluid sinks.
Energy transferred by electromagnetic waves emitted by warm objects.
How quickly the temperature of an object falls; depends on the rate of energy transfer out.
Foam injected into the gap between two brick walls to trap air and stop convection.
Windows with two panes separated by a gap of air or gas with low thermal conductivity.
Thick fibreglass or wool layer in the roof space that traps air and reduces energy transfer.
A graph of temperature against time for an object as it cools.
A variable kept the same so that the test is fair.

mistakes.w: Insulation stops heat escaping.
mistakes.r: Insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating.

mistakes.w: Insulation stops the cold getting in.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred from hot to cold; insulation reduces the energy transferred out.

mistakes.w: Thicker walls have lower thermal conductivity.
mistakes.r: Thermal conductivity is a property of the material; thicker walls reduce the rate of energy transfer, not the conductivity.

mistakes.w: Lubrication gives the machine more energy.
mistakes.r: Lubrication reduces friction, so less energy is wasted by heating.

mistakes.w: High thermal conductivity materials make good insulators.
mistakes.r: Good insulators have a low thermal conductivity.

mistakes.w: In the practical the best insulator has the highest final temperature, without fixing the start temperature.
mistakes.r: Compare temperature drop over the same time from the same starting temperature.

mistakes.w: Double glazing works because glass is a good insulator.
mistakes.r: The gas or air gap between the panes has a very low thermal conductivity and reduces conduction.

mistakes.w: Foam in a cavity wall works because foam is warm.
mistakes.r: Foam traps air in small pockets, reducing conduction and preventing convection currents.

exam.q: State one way of reducing unwanted energy transfer in a machine with moving parts.
model: lubrication / oil the moving parts
exam.tip: One word answers are fine for 1 mark.

exam.q: Explain how lubrication reduces unwanted energy transfers.
model: reduces friction between moving parts
so less energy is dissipated by heating (to the thermal store of the surroundings)
exam.tip: Say what is reduced and where the energy would have gone.

exam.q: Which material, copper or fibreglass, has the higher thermal conductivity?
model: copper
exam.tip: Metals are good thermal conductors.

exam.q: Two houses are identical except that house A has thicker walls. Which house cools more slowly? Explain why.
model: house A
thicker walls give a lower rate of energy transfer through them
exam.tip: Always link thickness to rate of energy transfer.

exam.q: Explain why walls made from a material with low thermal conductivity reduce heating bills.
model: low thermal conductivity means lower rate of energy transfer through the walls
so the building cools more slowly
so less energy (fuel) needs to be supplied by the heating to keep it warm
exam.tip: Chain: conductivity -> rate -> cooling -> energy needed.

exam.q: Explain how cavity wall insulation reduces energy transfer from a house.
model: foam traps air (low thermal conductivity), reducing conduction
prevents convection currents in the cavity
exam.tip: Mention both conduction and convection.

exam.q: A student tests insulators by wrapping beakers of hot water. State two control variables.
model: volume of water
starting temperature / thickness of material / same beaker / same time / lid used
exam.tip: Give specific variables, not 'keep it fair'.

exam.q: Describe how the student could use their results to decide which material is the best insulator.
model: calculate temperature drop over the same time for each material
the smallest temperature drop / least steep cooling curve is the best insulator
exam.tip: Refer to the same time interval.

exam.q: Suggest one improvement to the student's method and explain why it helps.
model: use a temperature sensor and data logger / repeat and find mean / use a lid
reduces reading error / improves repeatability / reduces energy lost by evaporation and convection
exam.tip: Improvement plus reason.

exam.q: Describe how the thickness and thermal conductivity of a building's walls affect its rate of cooling, and explain how a homeowner could reduce the rate of cooling of their house.
model: thicker walls lower the rate of energy transfer, so the house cools more slowly
walls of lower thermal conductivity lower the rate of energy transfer, so the house cools more slowly
loft insulation traps air and reduces energy transfer through the roof
cavity wall foam traps air and stops convection in the cavity
double glazing: gas gap with low conductivity reduces conduction
draught excluders reduce convection of warm air out of the house
exam.tip: Cover both factors from the spec, then several methods each with a mechanism.

worked.q: Explain why a house with single-brick walls and no loft insulation has much higher heating bills than one with cavity wall and loft insulation.
steps: Identify the energy transfer: energy is transferred from the warm house to the cold surroundings through walls and roof.
Single brick walls are thinner and the cavity is not filled, so the rate of conduction and convection is higher.
Without loft insulation, energy escapes through the roof at a high rate (warm air rises).
Cavity foam and loft insulation trap air, which has a very low thermal conductivity, reducing the rate of energy transfer.
So the insulated house cools more slowly and the heating must supply less energy.
worked.ans: The uninsulated house transfers energy to the surroundings at a higher rate, so it cools faster and needs more energy (higher bills) to stay warm.

worked.q: In PAG P5, water in beaker A (no insulation) falls from 80 °C to 52 °C in 10 minutes. Water in beaker B (2 layers of wool) falls from 80 °C to 66 °C. Compare the results.
steps: Rate of cooling A = 28 / 10 = 2.8 °C per minute
